title: The spacing effect
context: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

lines.t: Today I want to talk about something that can directly help you as students. It's called the spacing effect.

The spacing effect is the finding that we remember information better when we study it in several shorter sessions spread out over time, rather than in one long session. That one long session is what we usually call cramming.

This was first described more than a hundred years ago by a German researcher, Hermann Ebbinghaus. He tested himself by memorizing lists of nonsense syllables, short made-up words like dax or wib. He used nonsense words on purpose, so that his earlier knowledge couldn't help him remember.
He found that if he spread his practice over several days, he needed fewer total repetitions to learn a list than if he did all his practice on one day.

Why does spacing work? One explanation is that when you return to material after a break, you have partly forgotten it. Having to work a little to remember it again actually makes the memory stronger.
So here's a practical tip. Instead of studying for six hours the night before the exam, try one hour a day for six days. It's the same total time, but you'll probably remember much more.

title: Finding planets by transit
context: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.

lines.t: For most of history, we had no direct evidence that planets existed outside our solar system. Today we know of thousands. So how do astronomers find planets that are far too small and dim to see directly? I'll focus on the most productive technique, the transit method.

A transit happens when a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view. The planet blocks a tiny fraction of the star's light, so the star appears to dim very slightly, and then returns to normal once the planet has moved on.

How slight? If a distant observer watched Earth cross in front of the Sun, the Sun would dim by less than one hundredth of one percent. That's why space telescopes are so valuable: above the atmosphere, they can measure brightness extremely precisely.

From a transit, we can learn quite a lot. The amount of dimming tells us the planet's size relative to its star: a bigger planet blocks more light. And the time between transits tells us how long the planet takes to complete an orbit.

But there's a major limitation. A transit only occurs if the planet's orbit is lined up almost exactly edge-on from our viewpoint. Most planetary systems are tilted at some other angle, so their planets never pass in front of their stars as seen from Earth. That means for every planet we detect this way, there are many others we simply miss.

title: Tree-ring dating
context: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.

lines.t: Today's topic is a dating method that comes not from a laboratory but from trees. It's called dendrochronology, which simply means tree-ring dating.

You probably know that many trees add one growth ring each year. What's less well known is that the rings aren't all the same width. In a warm, wet year, a tree grows a lot and produces a wide ring. In a cold or dry year, the ring is narrow.

Because the weather affects all the trees in a region in a similar way, trees growing in the same area during the same years share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings. It's a bit like a barcode for a particular stretch of years.

Researchers have built long master sequences by overlapping these patterns. They start with living trees, whose outer rings can be dated exactly, then match their inner rings to the outer rings of older timber, say from an old barn, and then match that to even older wood from archaeological sites. In some regions, these chains reach back more than ten thousand years.
So if archaeologists find a wooden beam in an ancient house, they can compare its rings to the master sequence and often identify the exact year the tree was cut down.
Notice, though, that this tells us when the tree died, not when the house was built. Builders sometimes reused old timber, so archaeologists have to be careful in interpreting the dates.

Correct. The talk explains dendrochronology and how it dates wood.

title: Keystone species
context: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.

lines.t: Today we're going to talk about keystone species. The term comes from architecture. In a stone arch, the keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the very top. If you remove it, the whole arch falls down.
In ecology, a keystone species is a species that has a much bigger effect on its environment than you'd expect from its numbers. Remove it, and the whole ecosystem can change dramatically.
A well-known example is the sea otter on the Pacific coast of North America. Sea otters eat sea urchins. Sea urchins eat kelp, which is a large seaweed that forms underwater forests.

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, sea otters were hunted for their fur until they almost disappeared from many areas. Without otters, sea urchin populations exploded. The urchins ate the kelp, and in many places the kelp forests were replaced by bare rocky areas.
This mattered because kelp forests are home to many fish and other animals. So losing one species, the otter, led to the loss of a whole habitat.

When otters were protected and returned to some areas in the twentieth century, the urchins declined and the kelp forests grew back. That recovery is strong evidence that the otters really were playing a keystone role.

title: Rethinking the first-mover advantage
context: Listen to part of a talk in a business class.

lines.t: There's a widely held belief in business that the first company to enter a new market has a decisive advantage. It's called the first-mover advantage, and the reasoning sounds compelling.

A first mover can build brand recognition before anyone else, secure the best suppliers and locations, and, in some industries, create switching costs, meaning customers find it inconvenient or expensive to change to a competitor once they've adopted a product.

But when researchers actually examined market histories, the picture turned out to be far more mixed. Many pioneers failed outright, and in quite a few markets the eventual leader was a later entrant. Think of internet search. Several search engines were operating before the company that came to dominate the market even existed.

Why might arriving second be an advantage? For one thing, late entrants can learn from the pioneer's mistakes without paying for them. The pioneer bears the cost of educating customers about an unfamiliar product, of testing which features matter, and of discovering what doesn't work. A follower can observe all of that and enter with a more refined product.
There's also the matter of technology. A pioneer may lock itself into an early design, while a follower can adopt a newer one.

So the more accurate lesson isn't that being first is good or bad. It's that timing alone rarely determines success. Execution, meaning how well a company actually delivers its product, tends to matter more.

title: Flying buttresses and Gothic light
context: Listen to part of a talk in an architecture class.

lines.t: In our last session we looked at Romanesque churches, with their thick walls and small windows. Today we'll see how Gothic builders solved the problem that made those walls necessary.

The problem is this. A stone vault, the arched ceiling of a church, is extremely heavy, and it doesn't just push straight down. It also pushes outward, against the tops of the walls. Romanesque builders resisted that outward push with sheer mass. Their walls were thick, and they couldn't cut large openings in them without weakening them.

Gothic builders took a different approach. They used the pointed arch, which directs more of the weight downward than a rounded arch does. And they added the flying buttress: an external arm of stone that reaches from the upper wall out to a heavy pier standing away from the building. The buttress catches the outward push and carries it down to the ground outside.

Once the walls no longer had to carry all that force, they could be thinner and taller, and much of their surface could be given over to windows. That's what made the enormous stained-glass windows of the great cathedrals possible.
So when you look at a Gothic cathedral, the light inside and the forest of stone arms outside are really two sides of the same engineering solution.

title: The tragedy of the commons
context: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.

lines.t: Today I want to discuss an idea called the tragedy of the commons. Imagine a pasture that's open to all the herders in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more cow, but the cost, the damage to the grass, is shared by everyone. So each person has a reason to add more cows, and eventually the pasture is overgrazed and becomes useless to all of them.
For a long time, many economists concluded that there were only two solutions: either the government controls the resource, or it's divided into private property.

But the political scientist Elinor Ostrom challenged that conclusion. She studied real communities around the world, fishing villages, mountain pastures in Switzerland, irrigation systems in Nepal, and found that many of them had managed shared resources successfully for centuries without either solution.

What did these communities have in common? Among other things, clear boundaries about who could use the resource, rules created by the users themselves, monitoring by people who were accountable to the community, and penalties that started small and increased for repeat offenders.
Ostrom's work earned her the Nobel Prize in economics in two thousand nine. Her main point was not that the tragedy never happens. It's that it isn't inevitable.

title: How infants tune in to speech sounds
context: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.

lines.t: Let's turn to a striking finding about how infants perceive speech. Every language relies on a particular set of sound distinctions. English distinguishes r and l, for example, while Japanese doesn't treat them as separate sounds. Hindi, on the other hand, distinguishes two t sounds that English speakers typically hear as identical.
So researchers asked: are babies born tuned to their parents' language, or do they start out more open?

Since infants can't tell us what they hear, researchers used an ingenious technique. A baby learns that when a sound changes, an interesting toy lights up nearby. If the baby turns toward the toy right as the sound changes, we can infer that it noticed the change.

The results were remarkable. At six to eight months, English-learning infants distinguished the Hindi sounds about as well as Hindi-learning infants did. By ten to twelve months, however, their performance had dropped sharply, while the Hindi-learning babies remained accurate.
So the babies are actually losing an ability?

In a sense, yes, though I'd frame it as specialization rather than loss. The brain is committing its resources to the contrasts that matter in the language around it. That makes perception of the native language faster and more efficient, at the cost of sensitivity to contrasts that, for that child, carry no meaning. And it's not irreversible. Adults can regain some sensitivity with training, though usually with considerably more effort.
